newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Cautious businessman seen taking Hong Kong helm.
newsitem.headline: Cautious businessman seen taking Hong Kong helm.

text.p: A clearer picture is emerging of things to come when freewheeling Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to China next year.
Barring scandals, accidents or gaffes, a politically-conservative Hong Kong businessman whose family shipping empire was bailed out by Beijing in the mid-1980s, is poised to govern.

It is also anticipated that Hong Kong's most senior public servant will remain at her post as his deputy and main adviser, in a signal to a wary Hong Kong he wants minimal upheaval in the delicate weeks and months following the handover.
At midnight on June 30 next year, the British haul down their flag and hand over Hong Kong, a wealthy community of six million people, many of them refugees from China.

Shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa's landslide on Friday in the first round of the ballot by a China-appointed committee to choose Hong Kong's first post-colonial Chief Executive, leaves him poised for victory.

The deciding run-off between the three candidates who made it through the first round is scheduled for December 11 but Hong Kong media are already treating Tung as heir-apparent to outgoing British Governor Chris Patten.
They are urging the previously reclusive Tung to reveal more about his hopes, plans and aspirations.

"Even if the identity of the future Chief Executive appears clear...the people of Hong Kong can only benefit from hearing more of what he plans and getting his answers to questions that concern them," the South China Morning Post said.

Tung moves at his own pace. Despite months of speculation, he refused to be drawn on whether he would stand for the Chief Executive post, declaring his candidacy at the last minute and taking his time over preparing a policy platform.

The 59-year-old shipowner, a former adviser to both China and Britain, is the choice of the powerful business lobby, particularly if he forms a "dream team" with incumbent Chief Secretary Anson Chan -- Hong Kong's top civil servant.
Chan, dubbed the iron lady by the media, is held in high regard in Hong Kong. Opinion polls revealed her to be the favoured candidate for the top job but she declined to stand.
She has said publicly she is willing to stay on at her post and privately, her aides say, she is more than willing to work with Tung whom she knows well.
"She serves as a barometer. If she were to pack up and leave, it would be taken as a sign things had gone wrong, seriously wrong," said a close colleague and friend recently.
Maintaining Chan in her post would signal minimal change in the all-important 180,000-strong civil service.
The civil service runs Hong Kong and its senior members, not politicians, serve as policy-makers. An exodus from their ranks would pose a serious danger to stability.

In his policy platform Tung stressed the importance of the economy and put strong emphasis on what he called Chinese values -- the obligations of the individual to the community rather than rights of the individual.

Tung's innate conservatism is welcomed by the business community but worries members of Hong Kong's vocal pro-democracy camp who fear seeing the clock being turned back and the recent march towards greater democracy slowed.
His platform contains nothing that would offend China. He is willing to work with the controversial Provisional Legislature to be installed in place of the present elected chamber.

China was infuriated by electoral reforms spearheaded by the British in the early 1990s and vowed to dissolve the legislature in the face of adamant opposition from Hong Kong's vocal pro-democracy lobby.
